ket_qua.statement: Mawsynram, a village (in fact a cluster of villages) in the Khasi Hills of the state of Meghalaya, lies in the hills of northeast India.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Mawsynram is in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, although the description as a cluster of villages is less clearly established than its identification as a town and surrounding village area.

ket_qua.statement: Mawsynram is in the East Khasi Hills district of Meghalaya, India, at about 1,431 m on the southern edge of the Meghalaya (Khasi) plateau, above the low plains of Bangladesh's Sylhet region.
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: East Khasi Hills district; 1,431 m (4,695 ft); approximately 25°18'N, 91°35'E.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The WMO confirms the elevation and coordinates, while the district government confirms the southern plateau escarpment and the border with Bangladesh.

ket_qua.statement: Mawsynram is one of the rainiest places on Earth: the World Meteorological Organization lists it as having the greatest average annual rainfall in its Asia region (11,872 mm, 1941–1979).
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: 11,872 mm (11.872 m) average annual rainfall; WMO Region II (Asia); 38 years, 1941–1979.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The WMO explicitly identifies Mawsynram as the holder of the greatest average annual rainfall record in its Asia region.

ket_qua.statement: The World Meteorological Organization lists Mawsynram, India, as the record for the greatest average annual rainfall in WMO Region II (Asia): 11,872 mm (467.4 inches), based on data from 1941 to 1979 (38 years of record).
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: 11,872 mm (467.4 inches); 38 years of record, 1941–1979; Mawsynram, India.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The WMO's regional extremes archive confirms the rainfall figure, location, elevation and 38-year observation period.

ket_qua.statement: An average annual rainfall of 11,872 mm corresponds to a water depth of about 11.9 metres (about 39 feet), more than the height of a typical three-storey house (roughly 9–10 metres).
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The conversion is mathematically correct, and a 9–10 m three-storey building is a reasonable illustrative comparison rather than a standardized building-height measurement.

ket_qua.statement: Whether Mawsynram is the wettest place on Earth is disputed: nearby Cherrapunji (Sohra) holds the WMO world record for the greatest 12-month rainfall (26,470 mm, August 1860 to July 1861) and has a comparable long-term average; Lloró and López de Micay in Colombia have reported higher average annual rainfall that the WMO has not evaluated; and in 2013 an India Meteorological Department official said it could not be concluded with certainty which place is wettest.
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: Mawsynram: 11,872 mm/year in the WMO regional record; Cherrapunji: 26,470 mm over 12 months (August 1860–July 1861); López de Micay: reported historical average of 12,892.4 mm/year; Lloró: reported historical average of 12,717 mm/year.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The distinction between the WMO's evaluated regional records and competing Colombian rainfall datasets makes the worldwide wettest-place designation dependent on the dataset and observation period; the specific 2013 IMD official statement was not independently verified.

ket_qua.statement: Mawsynram is not on the coast: the Bay of Bengal lies far to the south of the Meghalaya plateau, beyond the low, flat plains of Bangladesh.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Peer-reviewed geographical research places the Meghalaya Plateau near the Bangladesh border and describes the flat Bangladeshi lowlands extending southward to the Bay of Bengal, confirming that Mawsynram is inland rather than coastal.

nguon.title: Contrasting Features of Monsoon Precipitation Around the Meghalaya Plateau Under Westerly and Easterly Regimes

ket_qua.statement: During the summer monsoon, warm moist air from the Bay of Bengal flows north across the flat Bangladesh plains and is forced up the steep southern slopes of the Meghalaya plateau (Mawsynram lies at about 1,431 m, roughly 4,700 feet), where it cools and its moisture condenses into very heavy orographic rainfall.
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: The Meghalaya Plateau reaches approximately 2,000 m elevation; the cited research supports the Bay of Bengal–Bangladesh–southern Meghalaya orographic rainfall mechanism, but does not establish Mawsynram's stated elevation of 1,431 m.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Peer-reviewed studies support the northward transport of moist monsoon air through Bangladesh and forced uplift against the southern Meghalaya slopes, but the precise Mawsynram elevation in the claim was not independently verified.

nguon.title: Contrasting Features of Monsoon Precipitation Around the Meghalaya Plateau Under Westerly and Easterly Regimes
Variation in the orographic extreme rain events over the Meghalaya Hills in northeast India in the two halves of the twentieth century

ket_qua.statement: Satellite-based studies (Ohsawa et al. 2001; Romatschke and Houze 2011, cited by Sato 2013) found that rainfall around the Meghalaya plateau peaks from around midnight to early morning, associated with a nocturnal low-level wind from the Bangladesh plains striking the southern slopes; hourly records at Cherrapunji (1946–1949) also showed more rain from 1 to 7 a.m. No hourly rainfall data exist for Mawsynram itself.
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: Cherrapunji hourly observations from 1946–1949 show greater rainfall during 01:00–07:00 IST than 12:00–18:00 IST, particularly from April to October. Sato (2013) identifies an evening-to-early-morning rainfall maximum and a nocturnal low-level jet, but the specific Bangladesh-plains wind explanation should not be treated as conclusively established by all the cited studies.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The early-morning rainfall pattern is supported by historical IMD observations and satellite-based research, but the proposed mechanisms differ between studies, and the searched sources do not establish the absence of hourly Mawsynram records.

ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: Olan Singh Suin's statement was reported on January 7, 2024.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: A January 7, 2024 report quotes Mawsynram MLA Olan Singh Suin explaining that some high-altitude villages experience drinking-water shortages during the lean season because water does not accumulate and streams sometimes dry up in spring.

ket_qua.statement: Living root bridges are found in Khasi and Jaintia villages in the hills of Meghalaya, mostly on the lower slopes (a 2015–2017 survey found most between about 250 and 900 m).
ket_qua.gia_tri_dung: The majority of surveyed living root bridges were located between 250 and 900 metres above sea level.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: A 2019 peer-reviewed study documenting bridges surveyed between 2015 and 2017 confirms their distribution across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills and finds that the majority grow between 250 and 900 metres above sea level.

nguon.title: Living bridges using aerial roots of ficus elastica – an interdisciplinary perspective

ket_qua.statement: Living root bridges are made by guiding the aerial roots of the rubber fig tree (Ficus elastica) across a stream, often along bamboo or other supports, until they root on the far bank.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Scientific research and UNDP describe bridges made by guiding the aerial roots of Ficus elastica across streams, using bamboo structures to direct and support their growth toward the opposite bank.

nguon.title: Living bridges using aerial roots of ficus elastica – an interdisciplinary perspective

ket_qua.statement: Living root bridges can take longer than a single generation to build: estimates of how long one takes to become usable vary, with UNDP giving 20 to 25 years and Ludwig et al. (2019) describing a process over generations, decades to centuries, including a bridge still not at full function after 66 years; the bridges keep growing and strengthening over time.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: UNDP estimates 20–25 years for the process, while Ludwig et al. describe construction extending over decades or centuries and explain that the bridges strengthen through continued biological growth and root fusion; these estimates concern different stages of development.

ket_qua.statement: The Khasi are matrilineal: descent is traced through the mother, and by custom the youngest daughter (ka khadduh) is the custodian, not the individual owner, of the ancestral house and family property, which belong to the lineage; selling it traditionally requires the consent of her maternal uncles and brothers.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Research and reporting support matrilineal descent, the youngest daughter's custodial responsibilities over ancestral property, and customary restrictions on disposing of that property without family or maternal-uncle consent; the precise arrangements can vary between families.
